They demonstrated strange behaviors such as responding to "Hello." by making non-sensical tool calls.  In this blog post, we will try to determine why this happened.
Rather than investigating every model at once, in this blog post I'm going to focus my effort on Llama 3.2.

You probably know that modern neural networks can be pretty large, and that is why special GPUs with lots of memory are in high demand right now.  So how are we able to run some of these models on our computers, which don't have these special GPUs, using Ollama?
One reason is because Ollama uses
models, which are sort-of numerically compressed.  For example, the
.  Don't worry about what these are, but they require 16-bits to store each parameter.  On
you can see the quantization is listed as Q4_K_M.  At a high-level, this squeezes each 16-bit parameter down to 4-bits.  And somehow it still works!
Or does it?  Maybe this is why our tool-callling doesn't work?
One simple way to test this is to evaluate a quantized version versus a non-quantized version.  Luckily,

on HuggingFace happens to have both quantized and non-quantized models in a format that Ollama can process.  So we can evaluate both of them using Ed's Really Dumb Tool-calling Benchmark ™️ that I introduced in

Behind the scenes, LLMs need to be prompted in a
specific format to work well.  HuggingFace dubs this problem the
.  In response, they created "chat templates" which codify the format and live alongside the model to avoid any ambiguity.  Note: I call these "prompt templates".
We haven't had to worry about prompt templates at all, because Ollama has been taking care of templating for us.  Maybe its prompt templates are wrong, somehow?
To test this theory, we're going to build some code to query Ollama without relying on Ollama to format the prompt for us.  There are two purposes for this:
We will learn a bit how tool calling works and how it interacts with prompt templates.  I have a suspicion that prompt templates have something to do with the problem.

We will avoid a lot of code that has been hiding behind abstraction.  This is the downside of abstraction: it makes things easier to build, but it's harder to understand where the blame might lie when something fails.
Let's start by examining the suggested prompt template for Llama 3.2.  (We'll talk more about this
, but finding the right prompt template is not as easy as it should be.)  Here is a link to the
for zero-shot function calling in Llama 3.2, which is what we want.

messages, which are hidden instructions that are sent to the LLM.  They can provide instructions on how the LLM should behave.  In this prompt format, we can see that it also includes how and when the LLM should interact with tools.

That doesn't look like either of the prompt templates we used before.  After a bit of google-fu, we can see that it originated from this
Llama 3.1 documentation on "JSON based" tool calling
Why are there multiple prompt formats for Llama 3.1?
Why not use the prompt format for Llama 3.2, since we are using the Llama 3.2 model?
Let's try to answer the first two.  In

A Meta employee states that the

in the tooling is the correct one.  Fortunately, that's what we have been using in this blog post.  (It's almost as if I knew this in advance!)  But Ollama has been basing their prompts on the one from the model website.

The last question, "Why not use the prompt format for Llama 3.2?" is pretty easy to answer as well.  Llama 3.2's default prompt format responds using a pythonic function call syntax that Ollama doesn't support.  And, as we saw above, the Llama 3.2 prompt anecdotally did not seem to work well.

First, let's make a query and make sure that we get the right answer!
The result of the foobar function with an input of 30 is 32.
Second, let's take a peek at the prompt we sent to the LLM.

Cutting Knowledge Date: December 2023
Today Date: 21 September 2024

Help and converse with the user.  If and only if the user asks a question that
is relevant to one of the following functions, make use of them.  If none of
the functions can be used, answer the query as best you can.
Here is a list of functions in JSON format:
{"type":"function","function":{"name":"foobar","description":"Computes the foobar function on input and returns the result.","parameters":{"type":"object","required":["input"],"properties":{"input":{"type":"integer","description":""}}}}}
Alright, let's run it through Ed's Really Dumb Tool-calling Benchmark ™️.  We'll run the original Llama 3.2 model and the Llama 3.1 tooling prompt too for comparison.
# based on the llama 3.1 tooling prompt

The original Ollama prompt scored 1.6/4.0.
The official Llama 3.1 tooling prompt scored 2.26/4.0, and my customized prompt scored 3.59/4.0.  I'd say that is an improvement!
I do want to come clean.  I did not create that prompt template in one try.  It actually took many days of experimenting and a bit of debugging.
(I find that this is often a dilemma when blogging.  Keeping track of everything you did is difficult, time-consuming, and often not that interesting.)
Many things went wrong along the way, but here are a few issues that I remember:
is supposed to be for enabling llama's code interpreter, but I wasn't able to get the prompt to work well without it.
Llama has some weird rules for when to use
, and I got them wrong.  As a result, even though the initial prompt was correct, Llama could not "parse" the results to correctly build the final message.
is enabled, tool calls are supposed to start with
.  Somewhat oddly (in my opinion), Ollama prompts "rebuild" the tool call response from the parsed values, rather than using the original message.  As a result, I had to add in the
or sometimes the model got confused and could not build the final message.
In one template, I added an extra newline, and this caused a notable decrease in performance!
Let's recap all the things we had to do to get to this point:
We used the Llama 3.1 prompt template from the
We modified the wording of the prompt to improve its responses to non-tool-calls like greetings and arithmetic.
And this was all just to improve the performance of one single model.  I'm tired, aren't you?
Prompts are definitely part of the reason why building tool calling agents did not work in
But HuggingFace raised the alarm about this a long time ago!

Sadly, the Ollama developers did not get this memo.  Instead of adopting the template format that HuggingFace did, they decided to use their own Go templates.  On one hand, this is a natural decision since Ollama is written in Go.
But the negative impact of this decision is that

has to write a new prompt template for every model on Ollama.  Sure, someone has to write the HuggingFace chat templates too, but many models already have these now, and they are often written by the model developer.
Currently, it is the Ollama developers themselves who are creating these prompt templates.  Do you trust them to do this after seeing the performance of the
model?  I don't.  But I also can't blame them.  Messing with prompt formats is

properties.ariaLabel: what can we do about it permalink

children.value: What can we do about it?

Ollama should either adopt the HuggingFace templates or create a tool that can convert HuggingFace templates to Ollama templates.  The current system of manually converting templates is error prone and harmful, and I have not seen any acknowledgment of this.  In fact, Ollama developers have regularly provided unhelpful and misleading
Don't bind tools if you don't want a tool call.
could be doing more about the prompt problem.  For Llama, it appears that they (the benchmark developers) seem to have chosen a format and implemented it.
Llama 3.1 and 3.3 appear to be based on the Llama 3.1 website prompt
--- the same one that the bad Ollama one used --- while other versions use a generic prompt.

We don't know how or why they selected these prompts.  They also don't have an incentive or responsibility to experiment.  Perhaps there should be more incentive for model developers to fix the prompt templates in order to score better on the BFCL, but it doesn't seem like that is how things works today.
The Llama developers really needs to do a better job documenting its prompt formats.  There shouldn't be so much conflicting information.  Even after
about it the problem remains.  And maybe this is the real problem.  If it was unambiguous which template to use, Ollama, HuggingFace and BFCL would probably all be using the right template.
In the same github issue, it's clear that people can't reproduce Meta's experimental results either.  So maybe Meta just needs to get their act together on documentation and reproduction.

We largely got to the bottom of the problems in Llama 3.2, but this was just one of many models that performed poorly.  Are all of these models suffering from prompt template problems, or are there other problems as well?  Stay tuned to find out.
